title: e-WV - Early Histories of Counties and Towns
content: A project of the West Virginia Humanities Council. The exact location and date of the first settlement in present-day West Virginia are unclear. Morgan Morgan, a Welsh immigrant, is often credited with making the first settlement near Bunker Hill, Berkeley County, around 1731. However, there were already settlers in the area by then. Most people who settled in Western Virginia before the French and Indian War used this route. By 1719, Lord Thomas Fairfax became the sole owner, and his land included most of present-day West Virg... The first permanent European-American settlement in Jefferson County started in the early 1700s. Shepherdstown, located along the Potomac River in Jefferson County, was possibly settled by German immigrants around 1717, making it one of the earliest settlements in present-day West Virginia. Martinsburg, the county seat of Berkeley County, was founded in 1778 by Gen. Adam Stephen. Moorefield, the county seat of Hardy County, was chartered in October 1777 and is the fourth-oldest town in West Virginia.

title: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History
content: By 1640, New England’s population approached 14,000 and the region was the most populous in English North America.[[5]](https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/early-settlements#_ftn5). In 1660 there were three major clusters of settlement: New England with a population of approximately 33,000; the Chesapeake with 25,000; and the English West Indies with 66,000, half of whom were enslaved Africans.[[6]](https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/early-settlements#_ftn6). All along the expanding backcountry frontier, Irish, Scots, English, Welsh, German, and French colonists, together with enslaved Africans and American Indians, evolved locally distinctive societies where ethnic diversity and the continual arrival of new settlers were taken for granted.[[10]](https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/early-settlements#_ftn10).
